name: Tlacoyalco Popoloca / Ngigua de San Marcos Tlacoyalco
confidence_why: Every description of the language rests on one fieldworker: Stark & Machin 1977 describe two lexically assigned stress types (consonant stress, lengthening a consonant of the final syllable in about three-quarters of morphemes, and vowel stress, lengthening the final or next-to-last vowel), Stark & Luna Villanueva 2011 restate the same system with a different syllable division, and DiCanio 2012 and Adamou 2025 only repeat the 1977 account, so the record is uncontradicted but has a single source behind it.

catalog_quote: Tlacoyalco Popoloca, like Eastern Popoloca (Kalstrom and Pike 1968), has two types of word stress, consonant stress and vowel stress. Every (phonological) word has one or the other, but never both. The predominant contrastive feature of stress is length. ... Consonant stress is identified by length of the consonant of the stressed syllable. ... In nearly all words with consonant stress, the stress occurs on the ultima. When a suffix is added, the stress moves. ... There are three suffixes -- ną¹ we/our, ra¹ you/your, and ba² (animal) -- which do not cause this stress movement. ... Certain suffixes -- such as čhą³ small, ʔa² not, and ną¹³ my -- cause vowel stress to move to consonant stress on the ultima. ... Vowel stress is identified by the lengthening of the vowel of the stressed syllable. ... In a syllable with a two-vowel cluster, vowel stress occurs on the second vowel. ... As in the case of words with consonant stress, the addition of a suffix to a word with vowel stress may cause the stress to move. Vowel stress moves to the penult. ... Certain suffixes -- such as a² your (sg.) and e³ his/their -- cause consonant stress to change to vowel stress. ... A numerical comparison of consonant versus vowel stress shows consonant stress to be the most common; only about twenty to twenty-five per cent of the morphemes in our lexicon have vowel stress. Consonant stress has limited distribution in that it does not occur in a syllable with a tone sequence.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Language not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title (Machin/Stark & Stark 1977, 'Stress and tone in Tlacoyalco Popoloca') is exactly a word-stress description of this language. The Glottolog URL is dead and the live SIL PDF is could not be reached by automated download, but the SIL Archives entries 8576 (chapter) and 8769 (full volume PIL 54) were located and both PDFs downloaded from the the Internet Archive (Sept/Aug 2024 captures) into, with lines added. The scans have no text; pp. 69-73 were scanned (tesseract, 300 dpi, one at a time) and the stress pages checked against the page scan. Deciding statement (pp. 69-71): two length-cued stress types, one per word; consonant stress (the common type) on the ultima in nearly all words and shifting to the ultima under suffixation; vowel stress (20-25% of morphemes) on ultima or penult, moving to the penult under suffixation; suffix-specific type switches. Coding proposal: final (ultima) stress, length-cued, with a lexical consonant/vowel-stress contrast and morphological penult cases. Two further records surfaced during this search of works with stress in the title and are listed as items: the SIL audio companion (entry 57642, not downloaded, no text) and Kalstrom & Pike 1968 on Eastern (Atzingo) Popoloca (other variety, paywalled DOI, not read). The earlier on-disk Rosetta excerpt (pp. 72-83) does not contain the stress section; the new full scan does. No catalog source exists to supersede.

new_statements.quote: Todas las palabras ngiguas llevan acento. El acento en ngigua tiene la función de alargar la vocal de la penúltima sílaba de la palabra o una de las consonantes de la última sílaba, de las siguientes maneras: [3.1] Si una palabra tiene acento vocálico, se acentúa la vocal de la penúltima sílaba y la vocal acentuada tiene una duración prolongada. Si la última sílaba de una palabra empieza con vocal, la vocal de la penúltima sílaba es alargada. [...] [3.2] Cuando el acento alarga una consonante, la consonante alargada siempre pertenece a la última sílaba
new_statements.translation: All Ngigua words carry accent. In Ngigua the accent has the function of lengthening the vowel of the penultimate syllable of the word or one of the consonants of the last syllable, in the following ways: [3.1] If a word has vowel accent, the vowel of the penultimate syllable is accented and the accented vowel has prolonged duration. If the last syllable of a word begins with a vowel, the vowel of the penultimate syllable is lengthened. [...] [3.2] When the accent lengthens a consonant, the lengthened consonant always belongs to the last syllable

new_statements.rule_in_words: Right-edge-bound, duration-based accent of two types: consonant accent lengthens a consonant of the word-final syllable (the saltillo if there is one, else j in a cluster, else the n of an n-cluster, else the single onset consonant), while vowel accent lengthens the vowel of the penultimate syllable. Vowel accent is automatic when the final syllable is vowel-initial (ni.o, nchi.a, na.a); before a consonant-initial final syllable the choice between penult vowel accent (ta.thii.ta, naa.gua, daa.na) and final consonant accent (kathe, kachro, jinda) is lexical and is marked in the orthography by a double vowel. The accent stays at the right edge when suffixes are added (kathe 'huarache' > kathena 'mi huarache', n lengthened; ni'ngo 'iglesia' > ningua 'tu iglesia', u lengthened and saltillo lost). Stark & Machin 1977 analyse the same system as 'consonant stress' vs 'vowel stress' (p. 72, 79-80). Closest fixed-list label: final syllable (consonant type) alternating with penult (vowel type); cf. sister language San Juan Atzingo Popoloca, coded morphological (root-final) in the catalog.
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 3 (p. 11): words ending in two vowels almost always have vowel accent, but some consonant-accent words end in two vowels; then the two vowels form one syllable and the accent falls on a consonant of that last syllable (chrjuin 'bonito', kjui 'se fue',;kjaon 'seis', de.jua 'duerme', jai.kua 'rápidamente', jie 'grande'). 3.2.1: the saltillo always takes the accent; when a suffix moves the accent to a new syllable the saltillo is lost (1977 p. 79 gives the same rule: žo²ʔ·o² > žo·¹a²).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('la palabra'), including possessed forms with suffixes; the description is of the citation-form word; tone (three levels) is independent of accent (ch. 2). The 1977 paper treats the domain as the phonological word and notes phrase-level tone lowering only.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2011 grammar describes exactly the variety of San Marcos Tlacoyalco, municipio de Tlacotepec, Puebla (subject language code pls = Glottolog sanm1301), under the autonym Ngigua; the 1977 paper calls the same variety 'Tlacoyalco Popoloca' / 'Northern Popoloca'. Author-order note: Glottolog lists the 1977 chapter as Machin & Stark, but its running head, Adamou 2025 and DiCanio 2012 all give Stark & Machin.

new_statements.reading: One stress per phonological word, cued by length rather than pitch. The majority type (consonant stress, ~75-80% of morphemes) is on the ultima in nearly all words and re-aligns to the ultima after most suffixes; the minority type (vowel stress) is lexically on the ultima or penult and moves to the penult under suffixation; suffix-specific rules switch a word between the two types. For a stress-position catalog this is a predominantly final-stress language (ultima), with a lexical consonant/vowel stress contrast and a morphologically conditioned penultimate pattern; stress placement is largely predictable from word edge plus morphology, the type (consonant vs vowel) being the lexical part.

new_statements.rule_in_words: One stress per phonological word, cued by length (a lengthened consonant or a lengthened vowel), not pitch. Consonant stress (75-80 % of morphemes) lengthens a consonant of the last syllable: in nearly all words it is on the ultima and it re-aligns to the new ultima when a suffix is added. Vowel stress (20-25 % of morphemes) lengthens a vowel, in a two-vowel cluster the second vowel; under suffixation it moves to the penult. Which type a morpheme has is lexical, and specific suffixes switch a word from one type to the other. The dominant surface pattern is therefore final (ultima) stress, with a lexical consonant/vowel-type contrast and a penultimate pattern for vowel-stressed words in suffixed forms. The language also has three lexical tones (p. 73), and consonant stress does not co-occur with a tone sequence on its syllable (p. 71).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-level secondary stress is described. Phrase level (p. 89): 'Phrase stress occurs on the stressed syllable of the last phonological word. With the exception of the anger phrase, the phrase-stressed syllable has greater consonant or vowel length than any other syllable of the phrase.' Emphatic intonation raises the stressed syllable of the emphasized word about two tone levels (p. 90).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 70: three suffixes (na1 'we/our', ra1 'you/your', ba2 'animal') do not cause the stress movement; certain suffixes (cha 'small', a 'not', na 'my') switch vowel stress to consonant stress on the ultima; p. 71: suffixes a 'your (sg.)' and e 'his/their' switch consonant stress to vowel stress; consonant stress never occurs on a syllable with a two-tone sequence (one exception under Rule 6, suffix na 'my'); p. 84 Spanish loans: 'In most words, the syllable which was stressed in Spanish receives vowel stress when the word is used in Popoloca'; six loans shift so that 'the following syllable receives consonant stress'; p. 89: with personal nouns plus optional na 'my', 'stress remains on the noun'.
new_statements.identity_note: Stark & Machin 1977, note 1 (p. 92): the data are from San Marcos Tlacoyalco, north of Tehuacán, Puebla (about 2700 inhabitants), gathered in 1971 from two principal informants (Pedro Hernández Melchor and Natividad Gámez Sánchez); 'One other village of similar size, San Luis Temalacayuca, plus a few scattered hamlets speak a closely related dialect.' Merrifield's Introduction (p. 1) calls it 'a northern Popolocan language'. The chapter contrasts it with Eastern Popoloca (San Juan Atzingo; Kalstrom & Pike 1968) and Western Popoloca (Williams & Pike 1968), which are other varieties, not sanm1301.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction between sources, but a labeling and description difference worth recording. Stark & Machin 1977 (pp. 69-71, read here from the full volume) put consonant stress (the majority type) on the ultima in nearly all words and show vowel stress on a final single vowel in unsuffixed words (sa31ko·2 'jacket', nta3se·2 'coffee') that 'moves to the penult' under suffixation; Stark & Luna Villanueva 2011 (sec. 3, pp. 11-13, same first author) summarize the same system as 'alargar la vocal de la penúltima sílaba de la palabra o una de las consonantes de la última sílaba', with vowel-stress examples where the last syllable starts with a vowel (ni.o, chia.on, nchi.a, na.a). The two descriptions coincide under the 2011 syllabification (stressed vowel + following vowel = two syllables, cf. 1977 'vowel stress occurs on the second vowel' of a cluster and its syllable border 'immediately following the stressed vowel', p. 72); 2011 simply does not state the 1977 case of vowel stress on a lone final vowel. The existing catalog readings differ only in label: existing_statements[0] calls the 2011 account 'fixed: other position', existing_statements[1] calls the 1977 account predominantly final with a lexical consonant/vowel contrast; the present read supports the latter (fixed: final syllable, with the lexical two-type contrast and a morphologically conditioned penult pattern noted as refinements).

sources.quote: Los tonos que modifican / los vocales / kjín / í (un acento en el vocal indica tono alto) / Tono medio / kjin / i (la i sola indica tono medio) / Tono bajo / kji̱n / i̱ (una raya debajo de la i̱ indica tono bajo)
sources.locator: pp. 55-57 (p. 55 'Los tonos que modifican los vocales' kjín / tono alto; p. 56 Tono medio kjin; p. 57 Tono bajo kji̱n)
sources.note: Community alphabet primer: one illustrated page per letter/digraph, then three pages 'Los tonos que modifican los vocales' giving a three-way tonal minimal triplet kjín (tono alto, acute accent) / kjin (tono medio, unmarked) / kji̱n (tono bajo, underline) and the orthographic convention for each; no analysis beyond the three level tones.

tone.translation: The tones that modify the vowels: kjín — í (an accent on the vowel indicates high tone); Mid tone: kjin — i (plain i indicates mid tone); Low tone: kji̱n — i̱ (a line under the i̱ indicates low tone).
